https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Romania on Thursday shut down the Cernavoda nuclear plant due to record-low Danube river levels. Drought and record-low water levels have deepened fears of an energy crisis across Europe. Photograph: Daniel Mihăilescu/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Romania on Thursday shut down the Cernavoda nuclear plant due to record-low Danube river levels. Drought and record-low water levels have deepened fears of an energy crisis across Europe. Photograph: Daniel Mihăilescu/AFP/Getty Images Romania Romania shuts its last nuclear reactor as drought-hit Danube river drops to record low Cernavoda shutdown poses immediate problems for Moldova, which relies on Romanian power ​to cover its own electricity shortages Guardian staff and agencies Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.20 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 23.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Romania has been forced to shut down the last working ⁠reactor at its only nuclear plant after drought caused the Danube river to fall to record lows – a rare move that will immediately affect power supplies in neighbouring Moldova . Drought and record-low water levels have deepened fears of an energy crisis across Europe , which is facing a new summer heatwave. The drought-hit Danube, whose waters cool the Romanian plant in Cernavoda, already forced Nucelarelectrica to shut down ⁠one reactor ​in late July. Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous | Yiannis Baboulias Read more On Thursday the company said it needed to shut the second reactor “due to the significant and ongoing drop” in the river’s water level, and it did not foresee a restart in within the next 10 days. Nuclearelectrica’s two 706-megawatt reactors account for 20% of the country’s power ⁠output. Romania has declared a state of energy emergency throughout August and asked companies and households to reduce consumption during peak hours. Shutting down the reactor posed immediate problems for Moldova, Romania’s eastern neighbour, ⁠which has also endured low river levels and relies on Romanian power ​to cover up to 60% ​of its own electricity shortages. With Romanian ​imports now unavailable, Moldova faces the prospect of increased purchases from Ukraine, ​if Kyiv can supply the ‌power, buying more ​expensive power from ​western countries or imposing rolling power cuts. “I think we should be ready for a worsening situation, including power outages, although it’s hard to say for sure right now,” Moldovan energy expert Sergiu Tofilat told Radio Chisinau. Romania’s energy ministry said it had ⁠turned on a 330-megawatt lignite-fired power plant, adding it was also relying on increased ​wind generation and hydro power – based ‌on available water in reservoirs – to ‌make up for shortages. It has warned that as a last resort, large industrial users would have to face restrictions in the evening hours to save electricity. In early August, the government said carmakers Dacia and Ford would pause production in the country until 19 August to help with the power deficit. Nearly two-thirds of the Danube has seen flow rates drop to the lowest on record for a July in 34 years, according to analysis from the European climate change observatory Copernicus. The drought has hit nuclear power providers across Europe. France, which uses nuclear power to generate about 70% of its electricity, recorded a more than 20% shortfall in atomic production capacity this week, a record deficit caused by outages linked to drought, extreme heat and a jellyfish invasion, according to Agence France-Presse calculations based on Électricité de France (EDF) data. In total, 13 of the 57 reactors in EDF’s nuclear fleet were affected. Hungary, neighbouring Romania, has avoided a complete shutdown of its only nuclear plant, Paks, whose four reactors are also cooled by the Danube. But with the river expected to drop further, Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, said on Wednesday that the government had ordered the construction of a submerged wall, or weir, to try to control flows nears the plant. Two 80-metre (260 feet) barges are also being stationed at Paks that could be sunk to raise the water level. Paks, which usually provides about a third of Hungary’s electricity, has been partially shut down since late last month. The drought in Europe has been exacerbated by human-induced climate change, according to the World Weather Attribution group of scientists, who warn that the problem will worsen. The low levels of the Danube, Europe’s second-longest river, have also severely affected shipping along its 2,850km (1,770 mile) route stretching from western Germany to the Black Sea. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters Germany Chancellor vows to stay on for Germany’s ‘democratic future’ after latest loss to far-right AfD Merz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliament Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows Kate Connolly in Berlin Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDT First published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 08.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Germany’s beleaguered leader, Friedrich Merz , has vowed to keep his fractious coalition government together for the good of the country’s “democratic future” after his conservative party suffered a drubbing at the polls in two state elections. Merz, who has vowed to plough ahead with an unpopular reform agenda, dismissed speculation over his position, saying it was vital that he and his coalition government remained in place. 10:54 Rise of the far right in Germany: how worried should we be? – The Latest Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows Read more “We are determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing,” Merz said on Monday. “It is about nothing less, and nothing more, than the democratic future of our country.” Germany faces political uncertainty in the aftermath of three hefty defeats for Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) this month, with it ousted from a state parliament for the first time, and the far right and far left making strong gains at its expense. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election 2026 results On Sunday the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged victorious in the coastal northern state ofMecklenburg-Western Pomerania for the third time in a German state, securing 38%. The anti-immigration, pro-Russia AfD party’s leaders predicted Merz would be out of office in months, as they set their sights on securing victory at the next federal election in 2029. “The chancellor certainly won’t make it to the end of the year,” Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s top candidate in Mecklenburg, said. “I think the twilight of the chancellor’s era has begun.” View image in fullscreen The AfD’s Leif-Erik Holm, Kristin Brinker, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla after the state election results. Photograph: snapshot/Future Image/B Elmenthaler/Shutterstock Merz described the results as a “disaster” , in particular the CDU’s ejection from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament, where it failed to reach the 5% barrier needed after losing more than half of its voters to the far-right AfD and centre-left Social Democrats. The result was all the more shocking as Mecklenburg was once a CDU stronghold. In Berlin on Sunday, the CDU fell to second place behind the far-left Linke party, which is on track to lead the next government in the city-state and could give Berlin its first Turkish-born mayor in its lead candidate, Elif Eralp. Berlin results chart In Mecklenburg, the SPD under its existing state leader, Manuela Schwesig, is expected to lead a three-party coalition government. Her campaign had focused almost wholly on presenting herself as a buttress against the AfD, as well as distancing herself from the federal government’s reform agenda. The SPD is Merz’s coalition partner in the federal government. Although the CDU’s poor performance had been predicted, Sunday’s outcomes only added to the extreme pressure on Merz already after the CDU’s crushing defeat to the AfD in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, which triggered the first serious speculation over his future as leader. Last week, the CDU’s powerful regional leaders governing in eight states gave their backing to Merz, but questions remain as to how sustained their support will be. At the same time there appear to be few candidates willing to step up to the post, which is increasingly being viewed as a poisoned chalice. On Monday, Merz dismissed the idea that the outcome was a personal rebuke. “The reasons for these election results go far beyond my own person,” he said. “We are witnessing a profound transformation of the political party system in Germany as well as in many other countries around the world.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Karin Prien, the CDU’s deputy leader, listening to Friedrich Merz in Berlin a week before the latest state elections. Photograph: Nadja Wohlleben/Reuters Karin Prien, the education minister and deputy CDU leader, accepted accusations that the government was failing to take voters’ fears seriously enough. But she said the government had no choice other than to continue trying to reform Germany from within, at a time of chronic economic weakness and global instability. “Without support and steadfastness we will not be able to achieve the necessary reforms, which are by no means a given. Nevertheless, not everything can remain as it is,” she told the broadcaster Deutschlandfunk. “The chancellor knows he will have to change, at least in how he addresses the people … We are a strong country, we have every chance of mastering this challenge together, but I believe that cooperating with each other will be crucial for this, and for the party it means we must broaden our appeal.” Doubts over the efficacy and fairness of the government’s agenda – which includes an overhaul of the pension system, a reduction in overbearing bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for the less well-off – played heavily into both election campaigns. On Monday, SPD leaders said they remained confident in their coalition with the CDU, but said that changes to the agenda were necessary. View image in fullscreen The SPD’s Lars Klingbeil flanked by his party co-leader Baerbel Bas (left), and Manuela Schwesig, the state leader in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Photograph: Christoph Rutenkolk/EPA Lars Klingbeil, the deputy chancellor and finance minister, said: “Saying we will ignore what the voters said to us in three state polls won’t work.” While the country needed reforms, he said, they “must be fair and they need support in the population”. The labour minister, Bärbel Bas, also of the SPD, said the plans needed a “reality check”, but said “nothing would be more lethal than letting this coalition break apart over some technicality”. Rubbing salt into Merz’s wounds, the Kremlin on Monday waded into the election analysis, calling the AfD’s win in Mecklenburg a response to Berlin’s refusal to buy cheap Russian gas, which has jolted the economy and caused prices to soar, contributing to voter dissatisfaction. The Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said: “Naturally, Germans, ​or at ​least some of them, are looking for an alternative to the current authorities in order to improve their situation. That is a natural process.” Explore more on these topics Germany Friedrich Merz Europe Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) The far right news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Germany’s Merz ‘grateful’ centre-left SPD wants to stay in coalition after CDU’s heavy losses – as it happened Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections Future of German chancellor hangs in the balance as two states go to polls Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy. https://ivn.us/win-or-lose-independent-c.text: Independent Candidates Win or Lose, Independent Candidates Are Building Something Bigger As a historic number of credible independents head into November, organizer Sarah Czech says the real work starts after the votes are counted. By Matt Shinners South Dakota Independent US Senate Candidate Brian Bengs. Image obtained from the candidate's Facebook page. Use of it does not equal endorsement from IVN. Published: October 06, 2026 Last updated: October 07, 2026 | Share Share to X Share to Bluesky Share to Facebook Share to LinkedIn Share by email When Sarah Czech and her team went door to door in Rapid City, South Dakota, last month, they were inviting complete strangers to come talk politics. Around 15 to 20 of them came to each event. "They came in and they were a little skeptical, but they left with a huge smile on their face," Czech said. "They were giving hugs to everybody." Czech works at the intersection of two kinds of organizations that have been quietly growing alongside this year's independent candidates . She is an associate at the Osmanthus Group, a consulting firm that works with independent campaigns, and since late August she has also worked on contract with Moving America Forward (MAF). Her view from the doorstep offers a look at a question hanging over the whole independent movement this cycle: what happens to the energy these candidates have generated, win or lose? An unusual year, and an infrastructure catching up There are more serious, well-funded independent candidates on the ballot this year than in any recent cycle. In Czech's estimate, it may be more than ever before. In South Dakota, Brian Bengs became the sole challenger to Republican Sen. Mike Rounds after Democratic nominee Julian Beaudion suspended his campaign in August. In Nebraska, Dan Osborn is again mounting a high-profile independent Senate run. Idaho has an unusual cluster: Todd Achilles for U.S. Senate, Sarah Zabel in the 1st Congressional District , and former state Supreme Court Justice John Stegner for governor. Around those campaigns, a support structure has started to form. National organizations such as the Independence Center, Unite America, and the Forward Party are working on the movement's ideas and its national profile. Newer groups are offering campaign services. Caroline Anderson has spent years working on campaigns, and in January she expanded her practice into the Osmanthus Group, bringing Czech on as her associate. Czech said what the national infrastructure still lacks is people knocking on doors and talking to voters one-on-one. "Obviously that requires money, and that requires time and all these other things," she said. MAF's events are designed to fill part of that gap. What South Dakota said back The Rapid City trip was a first look at a small Western city for many members of the team, who live in Boston, San Diego, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. Czech said that was part of the value. "We can be so caught up in the hyperpartisan warfare of what's going on when you are involved in the political movement that it's hard to take a step back and see things through the eyes of somebody who is not involved in this as much as we are," she said. The people who showed up were not activists. They considered themselves independent, but most were not deeply engaged in politics. Attendees ranged from 18-year-olds starting college to people in their 80s talking about their grandchildren. Some told the team they had not left their house in months, and that this was the first time anyone had invited them to something political that felt positive. Czech paused while recounting this to say it was emotional to talk about. The word Czech heard most often was "hope." One attendee, a man who had protested the Vietnam War in South Dakota decades ago, told the team that his generation had stood up and done the work in its time, and that now he needed to encourage his daughters that it was theirs. On issues, Czech hears independents gather around the national debt; the war in Iran and foreign policy more broadly; health care; and political reform; along with the economy and corruption, which she said matter especially in mountain states like Idaho and South Dakota. "We all really want to be able to afford gas, and we all really want to be able to afford groceries," she said. But she sees the deeper common thread as orientation rather than any single position. "Where Republicans and Democrats and conservatives and progressives are united against issues, I see independents united for something," Czech said. That something, in her telling, is love of country and community, and the question of how to protect and improve them. She also heard frustration with a broken bargain, particularly from registered Republicans. Several told her they had voted for what they thought would lower their prices, and felt that the opposite had happened. Czech described what she saw as a lack of trust rather than active distrust: skepticism toward politicians in general, and uncertainty about what a candidate without an R or a D next to their name actually means. That uncertainty is a hurdle at the ballot box, she said, but an asset across the dinner table. Partisans struggle to hear each other through the caricatures they hold of one another. An independent arrives without one. "There isn't a national caricature built around us, and so the masks can come down," she said. Why having real candidates matters Czech said the candidates have changed what outreach looks like. She recalled Unite America staff telling her that when they began organizing around the independent identity in 2017, people's reaction was flat refusal to engage. Now, she said, organizers can point to someone specific. "There is literally somebody who's viable and not scary and not crazy and [not] weird that is running in your area," she said. Voters often arrive already knowing the names, Czech said, citing Bengs, Achilles, and Zabel. She credited Bengs directly for the South Dakota trip, saying the team went to Rapid City only because he gave them an example to show people. "That's what they provide," she said. "A clear example of what an independent leader could look like." Idaho next, and the work after November The team heads to Idaho October 10–13. Czech is especially optimistic there: where many states have one viable independent, she said, Idaho has several . South Dakota taught logistical lessons, like the fact that apartment buildings in snow country are locked, unlike open-air complexes in Southern California, so canvassers need a local contact before they arrive. The bigger lesson was about priorities. Czech said organizations can get fixated on RSVP counts, but the point is the people who actually show up. "We're leaving, but they live there," she said. "We have to encourage them to be builders in these cities." That shapes MAF's plans after Nov. 3. The team intends to contact everyone it met, starting with a survey on the issues people care about and how they want to stay involved, and then help them form local chapters so that places like Boise and Rapid City become hubs for independent organizing. "Candidates and elections are temporary, but this movement is lasting," Czech said. Asked how to sustain hope if none of these candidates win, Czech acknowledged that disappointment would be real. But she pointed to what now exists that did not before. She has about 20 people in Rapid City she can text. Her message to them, she said, would be simple: two years ago, you had no one. Now, there are 20 of you. Two years from now, there could be 200. For a movement long defined by voters who belong to nothing in particular, that may be the most consequential result of this cycle, whatever the returns say on election night. https://telex.hu/direkt36/2026/10/25/meg.text: Menü Kereső Ránk számíthattok! 3000 új támogatót keresünk Csatlakozom Megbírságolták a Szent Imre Kórházat, ahol későn ismerték fel egy idős nő halálos infarktusát Direkt36 Belföld Legfontosabb Marton Kamilla Direkt36 Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A Direkt36 írta meg részletesen egy 89 éves, de életerős nő, Piroska történetét, aki nem kapott állapotának megfelelő ellátást a kórházban, és néhány órával később meghalt. Két év telt el Piroska halála óta, a Szent Imre most először fejezte ki részvétét a családnak. Szakmai hiányosságokat és dokumentációs szabályszegést állapított meg a Nemzeti Népegészségügyi és Gyógyszerészeti Központ (NNGYK) a Dél-Budai Centrumkórház Szent Imre Egyetemi Oktatókórházban. Az NNGYK azután kezdte vizsgálni a kórházat, hogy egy szívinfarktusban elhunyt idős nőnek a fia gondatlannak találta édesanyja ellátását, ezért hivatalos panaszt nyújtott be a hatóság felé. „Hivatalunk 500 000 forint egészségügyi bírságot szabott ki – amelyet az intézmény rendezett –, és kötelezte a szolgáltatót a szakmai szabályok maradéktalan betartására, különösen a kórházi felvétel indokoltságának megalapozott elbírálására” – írta az NNGYK a Direkt36 megkeresésére. Ahogy azt korábban részletes cikkben bemutattuk , Piroska 2024 szeptemberében került a Szent Imre Kórház sürgősségi osztályára, mert éles, sugárzó hátfájdalmat, fulladást és halálfélelmet tapasztalt. A triázst, azaz a sürgősségire érkező betegek állapotának felmérését végző ápolók a kivizsgálása során azonban nem végeztek EKG-t, hiába kérte a nő. Mivel a kórházban egyre romlott Piroska állapota, és hozzátartozói hiába kértek segítséget, úgy érezte, vesztegetik az idejét, és magánúton gyorsabban orvos elé kerülhet. Ezért az idős nő este fél tízkor saját felelősségre elhagyta a kórházat, néhány óra múlva azonban otthonában meghalt. Fia ezután nyújtott be hivatalos panaszt az NNGYK-hoz, amely több mint egy év várakoztatás után idén márciusban indított hatósági eljárást a kórház ellen. Vizsgálatuk arra jutott, hogy az EKG elmaradása „szakmai mulasztásnak tekinthető”, mert az EKG lehetővé tette volna, hogy gyorsan kiderüljön, hogy Piroskának szívinfarktusa van. Az NNGYK szerint az is szakmai mulasztásnak tekinthető, hogy az ápoló „kevésbé sürgős” esetként jelölte meg Piroskát. Ez azt jelentette, hogy akár 6-8 órát kellett volna várakoznia az orvosi vizsgálatig és a vérvétel eredményéig. A szakvélemény szerint a nő esetét „sürgősként” kellett volna meghatározni, ami alapján fél órán belül orvos elé kellett volna kerülnie. A fájdalmakkal küszködő asszony szeretett volna fájdalomcsillapítót is kérni, de nem adtak neki. „Azt otthon kellett volna bevenni” – mondta neki az egyik ápoló Piroska fia és barátnője szerint, akik végig az asszonnyal voltak halálának estéjén. Ahogy azt korábbi cikkünkben megírtuk, az NNGYK vizsgálata az ápoló kommunikációjára és a gyógyszer megtagadására nem tér ki, de az kiderült, hogy az ambuláns lapról hiányzik a fájdalom erősségének rögzítése. A hatóság vizsgálata szerint a nő által említett erős fájdalmak is inkább a sürgős besorolást indokolták volna. A történteket a Szent Imre kórház is vizsgálta még 2024-ben, de nem talált szakmai mulasztást. Ugyanakkor tudomásul vette az NNGYK márciusi vizsgálatának megállapításait, és arra is kitért, hogy „a betegekkel való nem megfelelő kommunikációt intézményünk semmilyen formában nem tartja elfogadhatónak”. Az ügy következménye lett az NNGYK által kiszabott 500 ezer forintos bírság és az, hogy a Szent Imre Kórház a sürgősségi ellátásban azóta több, a betegbiztonság növelését célzó intézkedést is bevezetett. Például ma már reggel és este 10 óra között a korábbi egy helyett egyszerre két dolgozó végzi a sürgősségire érkező betegek állapotának felmérését, azaz a triázst. Minden triázst végző szakember rendelkezik a szükséges végzettséggel, és folyamatban van a rendszeres oktatás bevezetése, amely a tudásuk frissítését szolgálja – közölte a kórház a Direkt36 megkeresésére. Ezen kívül az osztályvezető vagy annak helyettese a triázs során keletkezett dokumentumokat naponta átolvassa és ellenőrzi. Kéthetente összehívott osztálymegbeszéléseket is tartanak majd, amelyeken átbeszélik a mindennapi problémákat és a komplikáltabb eseteket. A Direkt36-nak írt válaszában a kórház részvétét fejezte ki Piroska családjának. Ez mintegy két évvel a halála után most először történt meg. Piroska fia vegyes érzelmekkel fogadta a bírság hírét és a kórház válaszát. „Örvendetes, hogy a hatóság megállapította a felelősséget, még ha ez a kiszabott 500 000 forintos bírság inkább csak jelképes összegnek tekinthető is a súlyos mulasztásokért cserébe” – mondta a Direkt36-nak. A férfi értékeli a kórház gesztusát és örül annak, hogy javítani szeretnének a betegbiztonságon. Ugyanakkor nem érti, hogy miért csak most vezették be az új intézkedéseket. „A tragédiát megelőzően semmiféle napi ellenőrzés és kontroll nem működött az osztályon? Eddig nem volt semmilyen visszacsatolás, nem reflektáltak a problémás esetekre, és nem vonták le a tanulságokat?” – kérdezte a férfi, és hozzátette, számára ijesztő felismerés, ha ezeket az alapvetőnek tűnő szakmai gyakorlatokat tényleg csak most vezették be.
